question.text:
Which of the following products is the LU factorization of a matrix $A?$

  1. $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -9 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$
  3. $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 6 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
question.explanation:
Remember that in the LU factorization of a matrix $A,$ we write $A=LU$ where the matrix $L$ is a unit lower triangular matrix (a lower triangular matrix that has only $1$'s on the main diagonal) and the matrix $U$ is an upper triangular matrix:

\[ A= \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}0} \\ \ast & {\color{blue}1} \end{bmatrix}}^{L} \cdot \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \ast & \ast \\ {\color{red}0} &\ast \end{bmatrix}}^{U} \]

With that in mind, let's inspect each product in turn.

  • The first product is in $LU$ form because the left matrix is a unit lower triangular matrix, and the right matrix is an upper triangular matrix. \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}0} \\ -9 & {\color{blue}1} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ {\color{red}0} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad {\color{green}\checkmark} \]

  • The second product is in $LU$ form because the left matrix is a unit lower triangular matrix, and the right matrix is an upper triangular matrix. \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}0} \\ 5 & {\color{blue}1} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 \\ {\color{red}0} & 8 \end{bmatrix} \quad {\color{green}\checkmark} \]

  • The third product is not in $LU$ form. Although we have a product of an upper triangular matrix on the left and a unit lower triangular matrix on the right, the order of multiplication is not correct (instead, we need a unit lower triangular matrix on the left and an upper triangular matrix on the right). \[ A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 6 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad {\color{red}\times} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

  1. $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
  3. $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$
question.explanation:
Remember that in the LU factorization of a matrix $A,$ we write $A=LU$ where the matrix $L$ is a unit lower triangular matrix (a lower triangular matrix that has only $1$'s on the main diagonal) and the matrix $U$ is an upper triangular matrix:

\[ A= \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}0} \\ \ast & {\color{blue}1} \end{bmatrix}}^{L} \cdot \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \ast & \ast \\ {\color{red}0} &\ast \end{bmatrix}}^{U} \]

With that in mind, let's inspect each product in turn.

  • The first product is not in $LU$ form because the matrix on the left is not a unit lower triangular matrix, as it has an entry not equal to $1$ on the main diagonal. \[A=\begin{bmatrix} \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{-1}& 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\quad {\color{red}\times} \]
  • The second product is not in $LU$ form because the matrix on the right is not an upper triangular matrix, as it has a non-zero entry below the diagonal. \[ A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{-1} & 2 \end{bmatrix} \quad {\color{red}\times} \]
  • The third product is in $LU$ form because the left matrix is a unit lower triangular matrix, and the right matrix is an upper triangular matrix. \[ A= \begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}0} \\ 2 & {\color{blue}1} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ {\color{red}0} & 2 \end{bmatrix} \quad {\color{green}\checkmark} \]

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

\[ B= \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}0} \\ \ast & {\color{blue}1} \end{bmatrix}}^{L} \cdot \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \ast & \ast \\ {\color{red}0} &\ast \end{bmatrix}}^{U} \]

With that in mind, let's inspect each product in turn.

  • The first product is not in $LU$ form because the matrix on the left is not a unit lower triangular matrix, as its main diagonal contains numbers different from $1.$ \[ B=\begin{bmatrix}\bbox[2pt,lightgray]{12} & 1 \\ 1 & \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{0}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}11 & 17 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad {\color{red}\times} \]

  • The second product is in $LU$ form because the left matrix is a unit lower triangular matrix, and the right matrix is an upper triangular matrix. \[ B= \begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}0} \\ 12 & {\color{blue}1} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 17 \\ {\color{red}0} & 1 \end{bmatrix}\quad {\color{green}\checkmark} \]

  • The third product is not in $LU$ form. Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

question.explanation:

\[ C= \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}1} & {\color{red}0} \\ \ast & {\color{blue}1} \end{bmatrix}}^{L} \cdot \overbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} \ast & \ast \\ {\color{red}0} &\ast \end{bmatrix}}^{U} \]

  • The first product is not in $LU$ form because the matrix on the left is not a unit lower triangular matrix, as its main diagonal contains a number not equal to $1.$ \[ C=\begin{bmatrix}\bbox[2pt,lightgray]{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad {\color{red}\times} \]

  • The second product is not in $LU$ form. question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 3 \\ 14 & -5 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

\[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 3 \\ 14 & -5 \end{bmatrix} & \quad R_2 &:= R_2 + 2R_1\quad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_1 A &= U \\[5pt] A &= E_1^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[5pt] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*}

To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $B$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $B$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

\[ \begin{align*} B &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 9 \\ 7 & 20 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + \left(-\dfrac{7}{3}\right)R_1\qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -\dfrac{7}{3} & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot B \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 9 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1B=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_1 B &= U \\[5pt] B &= E_1^{-1} U \\ B &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -\dfrac{7}{3} & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\ B &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \dfrac{7}{3} & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 9 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*} Therefore, $l_{21}=\dfrac{7}{3}, u_{12}=9,$ and $l_{21}\cdot u_{12}=21.$
